case_studies.title: Prune First, Decide Fast: Scalable Semantic Query Processing with JEVDB
case_studies.abstract: Semantic database systems extend SQL with foundation-model inference over unstructured data, but current engines rely heavily on autoregressive LLMs for discrete relational decisions, creating high latency and monetary cost. We present JEVDB, a scalable semantic database system that uses fast, typed decision models for semantic filters, joins, classification, and ranking, while selectively escalating uncertain cases to generative LLMs. To reduce semantic-join work, JEVDB combines exact Yannakakis-style semijoin reduction over relational structure with Semantic Bloom Filters (SBFs), which use r
case_studies.summary: JEVDB tackles the high cost and latency of semantic queries by using fast, typed decision models for most operations and only calling expensive LLMs when needed. It builds a scalable system that prunes joins with Yannakakis-style reductions and Semantic Bloom Filters, achieving faster responses and lower cost. For IT managers, the key takeaway is that this approach can make complex semantic queries cheaper and quicker if you can integrate it into your data stack.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage semantic query workloads, step 1: replace or augment your current LLM-heavy engines with a typed decision model for filtering, joining, and ranking; step 2: implement a Bloom filter layer to prune unlikely join candidates; step 3: route only uncertain results to the LLM to keep cost and latency down.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel semantic database system that combines fast typed decision models with selective LLM use, which could interest IT engineers working with data platforms and cloud databases. However, the concepts are still at an academic prototype stage and lack immediate, actionable deployment steps for typical IT infrastructure teams. Therefore the novelty score is moderate (20/33), the IT relevance is low‑moderate (15/33) and the practical value for quick implementation is minimal (5/34).
